comments.author: @RogerWKnight
comments.text: Interesting.  Seattle and Tacoma sit where river deltas meet deep water harbors.  Fill was used to create dry land on top of these tideflats while channels were dug to provide a place for the water of the Puyallup and Duwamish Rivers to flow and to provide docking locations for freight hauling ships.  We now have huge container ports at Seattle and Tacoma.  Soundings in the middle of Elliot Bay, Seattle, are over 300 feet, and over 150 feet right in front of the edge of Harbor Island.  Tacoma is like that too.  Could an event such as described here move half of Harbor Island to the middle of Elliot Bay?  Triggered by a Cascadia Full Rip earthquake of magnitude 9?  If so, it could cause a big chunk of Vancouver, its Airport, Richmond, Tsawwassen, and Point Roberts to fall into the depths of the Strait of Georgia.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: That’s a fair question, Roger. The Bute Inlet study observed small slides and explicitly left open whether larger failures would behave the same way. It doesn’t establish a scenario where whole neighbourhoods slide into deep water, those locations would each need their own assessment.

comments.author: @debragraceperi
comments.text: I'm surprised that the projected rate of displacement was linear. Especially considering the fluid dynamics of not only the water, but also the sediment as well. Surely this must be improved to be able to generate more accurate projections/predictions.

replies.author: @debragraceperi
replies.text: ​@HiddenCanadayes, I understand. What I'm saying is the model isn't representative of the actual physics.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: The movement actually paused, sped up and sometimes collapsed suddenly. The rates quoted describe what was observed, rather than a constant-speed forecast. Those departures from the models are part of what makes the measurements so useful!
